html:
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was an Austrian composer, born in Salzburg in 1756, who became one of the greatest figures of the Classical period in music. In a life of under 36 years he wrote more than 600 works in every major form of his day, including the operas The Marriage of Figaro and The Magic Flute.

He was a child prodigy. His father Leopold, a court musician, toured him and his sister around the courts of Europe from the age of six, to Munich, Vienna, Paris, London and Italy. He was writing symphonies before he was ten.

As an adult he chafed in the service of the Archbishop of Salzburg. In 1781 he quit and moved to Vienna, then the musical capital of the Holy Roman Empire, to live as a freelance: teaching, giving concerts and selling his music.

Main works:

  • Operas: The Abduction from the Seraglio, and three with the librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte, The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni and Così fan tutte; then The Magic Flute (1791).
  • Piano concertos he wrote to play himself, and 41 numbered symphonies.
  • Chamber music, including quartets dedicated to his friend Joseph Haydn.
  • The Requiem, left unfinished at his death.

Figaro, based on a play banned in Paris for mocking nobles, shows the mood of the years before the French Revolution. Money troubles dogged his last years, though his income was often good. He died in Vienna in December 1791 of an illness whose cause is still argued over. The young Beethoven came to Vienna the next year, hoping, as a patron put it, to receive Mozart's spirit from Haydn's hands.
